name: Malloy
vendor: Malloy project (LF Projects, started at Google by Lloyd Tabb’s team)
summary: A modelling and query language from Looker co-founder Lloyd Tabb that compiles to SQL: define joins and measures once in a source, then write short queries, including nested ones, that run on DuckDB, BigQuery, Snowflake, PostgreSQL and other engines.
intro: Malloy has two layers. A `source` is a semantic model on top of a table or query: it names joins, dimensions and measures, such as an on-time rate that excludes cancelled and diverted flights. A query starts from a source and lists what to `group_by`, `aggregate`, filter with `where` and sort; results are sorted by the first aggregate unless you say otherwise. Queries can be saved in the source as `view`s and refined later, and each query can serve as the source for the next, so analyses are built from small reusable pieces. The Malloy compiler turns all of it into SQL for the connected database and runs it there.

Two things set it apart from hand-written SQL. Measures stay correct across joins: Malloy tracks which table an aggregate belongs to, so a `sum` over a joined table doesn’t double-count rows that the join fanned out. And `nest:` puts a whole sub-query inside each result row, so “carriers, with their top airports inside each carrier” comes back as one result with an array per row; on DuckDB the compiler builds this in a single SQL statement using grouping sets and `LIST`. The README lists BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB, MotherDuck, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Trino, Presto and Databricks. Tooling includes a VS Code extension for writing models and charting results, npm packages, the `malloy-cli` command line (`run`, `compile`, `build`, plus an MCP server), and Publisher, a server that exposes models through REST and MCP APIs.
strengths: Business logic lives in one model, and every query reuses the same measures and joins instead of copying SQL
Aggregates stay correct across one-to-many joins without hand-written subqueries or `DISTINCT` tricks
Nested results in one query, useful for dashboards and for nested data such as arrays of records
Runs on the database you already have; `malloy-cli compile` shows the SQL it will send
limits: Another language to learn, with a much smaller community than SQL or dbt; BI tools and SQL clients don’t speak it, so you go through the VS Code extension, the CLI, Publisher or the npm libraries
Mostly for reading and analysing data, not for writes or DDL; `malloy-cli build` can create tables from queries
The npm packages are still versioned 0.0.x (0.0.435 in October 2026); the language itself has promised code compatibility since 4.0 in 2023
Generated SQL for nested queries is long and engine-specific, which makes it harder to read and tune than hand-written SQL

story: Lloyd Tabb co-founded Looker and was the lead inventor of LookML, the modelling language from which Looker generates SQL. After Looker became part of Google he kept working on the same problem there: SQL is complete, but verbose and without reusable parts, and real data is often nested rather than rectangular. With a small Google team he started Malloy, whose repository dates from August 2021; early versions compiled to SQL for BigQuery and PostgreSQL and were described as an experimental language.

The team added DuckDB, data notebooks and a command line, and wrote about the language’s design on its blog. Malloy 4.0, in October 2023, cleaned up the syntax (`extend`, `view:`, `run:`, `select:`) and dropped the word “experimental”, with a promise to keep existing code working. The project now lives under LF Projects, the Linux Foundation’s entity for hosting open-source projects, with committers listed in its contributing guide, and its newer work includes Publisher, MCP access for AI agents and tooling for writing models with LLMs.

choices.choice: Compile to SQL, don’t build an engine
choices.why: Data already lives in BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake and DuckDB. Generating SQL lets Malloy run where the data is and lean on each engine’s optimizer.

choices.choice: A semantic model in the language itself
choices.why: LookML’s lesson: measures and joins should be defined once. Malloy makes the model and the queries one language, so a query can extend the model and leave reusable pieces behind.

choices.choice: Nested results as a first-class feature
choices.why: Tabb argued that data isn’t rectangular. `nest:` returns hierarchies in one query, which also matches how dashboards drill down.

choices.choice: Break the syntax once, then freeze it
choices.why: Malloy 4.0 made all the incompatible changes in one release, with warnings in the VS Code extension first, so later versions could promise compatibility.

timeline.text: Release 0.0.435 (October); the CLI now includes an MCP server
